```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A Research Guide is not a monolith — it is assembled from small, composable
reporting functions, one stage at a time. This vignette opens the hood and runs
the whole pipeline on a **single raw vector**: guess its type, measure it, report
the numbers as a table, and draw the visual. `create_dgf()` does exactly this for
every column of a dataset at once; here we do it for one, by hand.

```{r lib, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(datagoodr)
v <- dg_demo$revenue   # a raw vector: dollar amounts
head(v)
```

## Stage 1 — guess the data type

Typing is the first move, and it comes from the companion package **formex**. Hand
it the vector (the column name is a useful hint) and read the `$route`:

```{r guess, warning=FALSE}
route <- formex::guess_data_type(v, name = "revenue")$route
c(data_type = route$data_type, semantic_type = route$semantic_type,
  depth = route$depth, confidence = round(route$confidence, 2))
```

A number, recognized from the values. The type is what selects every reporting
function that follows.

## Stage 2 — measure the column

The measurement functions take a variable name and a data frame and return the
profile as JSON — the exact payload datagoodr stores in the DGF's `rg_*` cells.
The **universal** quality counts:

```{r props}
df <- data.frame(revenue = v, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
get_properties("revenue", df)
```

and the **type-specific** statistics (here, the numeric quantile ladder plus
mean, skew, and kurtosis):

```{r stats}
get_stats("revenue", df, "numeric")
```

This JSON is the "inner" profile. Nothing about it is tied to how it will be
shown — reporting is a separate stage.

## Stage 3 — report the numbers as a table

To render, the profile is carried in a DGF and handed to a `dg_*` reporting
function, which parses the JSON and prints a table. Build a one-column DGF and
report the stats:

```{r dgf, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results="hide"}
dgf <- create_dgf(df, file = tempfile("dgf"), open = FALSE)
```

```{r table, results="asis"}
dg_properties(dgf, "revenue")   # the universal counts, as a table
dg_stats(dgf, "revenue")        # the numeric statistics, as a table
```

## Stage 4 — create the visual

The graphic is chosen by type too: `dg_graphic()` dispatches a number to the
histogram renderer, reading the same stored profile.

```{r plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=2.8, fig.alt="Histogram of the revenue vector"}
dg_graphic(dgf, "revenue", label = "")
```

## Putting it together

Four stages — **guess, measure, tabulate, visualize** — each a small function
selected by the column's type. A different vector would route through different
functions: a categorical column to `paste_treemap`, a date to the calendar
heat-map, free text to the word cloud. That type-to-function mapping is itself a
setting you can inspect and change — see *Report Aesthetics and Customization*.

`create_dgf()` runs stages 1–2 for every column and stores the result; the
Research Guide runs stages 3–4. Everything in this vignette is what happens inside
those two calls.
